findings.body: The code concatenates the untrusted userName into a shell command string passed to execSync, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands. This can lead to remote code execution on the server.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /'), which execSync executes, causing destructive actions.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by sanitizing user input

findings.body: execSync runs the command in a shell, so an attacker can inject shell commands via userName. The previous implementation used spawnSync with an argument array, which is safer. The new code also builds the command string unsafely. This can lead to arbitrary command execution if userName contains shell metacharacters. Also change the import to spawnSync.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes userName = "; rm -rf /;". The execSync call runs `report --user ; rm -rf /;`, deleting all files.
findings.title: Replace execSync with spawnSync to avoid shell injection

findings.body: The return statement now uses rows.slice(1), which removes the first element of the array. This changes the function's contract from returning all rows to returning all but the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows contains only one element, the function returns an empty array, which may break callers expecting at least one row.
findings.title: Function now discards the first row

findings.body: The call to candidate.strip_prefix(&root).map_err(|_| io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied)?; is incorrect. map_err converts the StripPrefixError into an io::ErrorKind, which does not implement std::error::Error, so the '?' operator cannot be applied and the code will not compile. Even if it did compile, the error is ignored, allowing a path outside the intended root to be opened, which is a security vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: If the supplied name resolves to a path outside the canonicalized root, strip_prefix will return an error. The current code ignores that error and proceeds to open the file, potentially exposing arbitrary files. Additionally, the '?' operator on io::ErrorKind causes a compile error, preventing the function from compiling.
findings.title: Handle strip_prefix error and prevent path traversal

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: Using Runtime.exec with a shell command concatenates user input directly into the command string, allowing command injection if the user contains shell metacharacters. The previous ProcessBuilder call passed arguments safely. This change introduces a security vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker supplies a user string like 'alice; rm -rf /', the shell will execute the injected command, potentially compromising the system.
findings.title: Avoid shell injection by using ProcessBuilder

findings.body: The method now returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()), which drops the first element of the list. The original implementation returned the full list. This change silently modifies the output, potentially breaking callers that expect the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: When the caller expects the first row to be present, the returned list will be missing it, leading to incorrect data processing or assertion failures.
findings.title: Do not discard the first row of the report

findings.body: The test now only checks that the result is not null, but does not verify that the returned list contains the expected rows. This reduces test coverage and may allow regressions to go unnoticed.
findings.failure_scenario: If the implementation changes to return an empty list or a different structure, the test will still pass, masking the bug.
findings.title: Verify returned rows instead of just non-null

findings.body: The test only checks that the result is not null, but does not verify that the report command is invoked without a shell. This leaves the spec requirement untested.
findings.title: Test does not cover shell invocation

findings.body: The new implementation filters items by Active status and Owner.Enabled, whereas the original returned all items. This deviates from the original behavior and likely from the intent to simply load items.

findings.body: Each iteration calls repo.Load(id), resulting in one database query per id. This scales linearly with the number of ids and can exhaust resources.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many elements, the function issues a separate round-trip per id, increasing latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: Avoid N+1 queries by batching repository loads

findings.body: ResultSliceFactory and its Create method are never used elsewhere and only provide an empty slice. They add unnecessary indirection.

findings.title: Avoid using pull_request_target with secrets

findings.body: The RELEASE_TOKEN secret is added to the environment of a step that runs code from the PR. In a pull_request_target workflow, this secret is available to the PR author, leading to secret leakage.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR author reads the RELEASE_TOKEN from the environment and can publish releases or access protected resources.
findings.title: Expose secret in workflow environment

findings.body: The validation only blocks the public CIDR 0.0.0.0/0 but allows any other CIDR, including public IPs. This can expose SSH access to the internet if an attacker sets admin_cidr to a public address. The rule is intended to restrict admin access to a private network, but the current validation is insufficient.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker sets var.admin_cidr to a public IP or CIDR (e.g., 8.8.8.8/32). The security group rule then allows SSH from that public address, granting the attacker remote access to the instance.
findings.title: Restrict admin access to private network only

findings.body: The variable admin_cidr only checks that it is not public, but accepts any string. An invalid CIDR could cause the security group rule to be created with an invalid CIDR, leading to deployment failure or misconfiguration.
findings.failure_scenario: When admin_cidr is set to an invalid CIDR string, Terraform may create a rule with an invalid CIDR, causing deployment failure or misconfiguration.
findings.title: Add CIDR format validation to admin_cidr variable

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.

findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by avoiding shell=True with untrusted input

findings.body: The loop calls repository.load for each item_id, causing a separate database query per item. This scales linearly with the number of items and can exhaust connections.
findings.failure_scenario: When item_ids contains many IDs, the function performs many round-trips, increasing latency and potentially hitting connection limits.
findings.suggestion:

    return results

findings.title: Avoid shell injection by not using sh -c

findings.title: Avoid using secrets in pull_request_target workflow

findings.body: The RELEASE_TOKEN secret is set as an environment variable in a workflow that runs on pull_request_target, which can be triggered by forks. This exposes the secret to untrusted code.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR from a fork can read the RELEASE_TOKEN secret and use it to publish packages or access protected resources.
findings.title: Do not expose RELEASE_TOKEN in pull_request_target workflow

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: execSync throws on non-zero exit codes, whereas spawnSync returned a result that was ignored. This change can cause the function to crash unexpectedly, breaking callers that relied on silent failure.
findings.failure_scenario: When the report command exits with a non-zero status, execSync throws an exception, causing the caller to crash instead of silently ignoring the error.
findings.title: Avoid silent error handling by using spawnSync or handling execSync errors

findings.body: execSync runs the command through a shell; interpolating userName directly allows shell metacharacters to be executed. The original spawnSync used a safe args array.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName contains shell metacharacters, an attacker can execute arbitrary commands, leading to privilege escalation or data loss.
findings.title: Prevent shell injection by escaping user input

findings.body: The function returns rows.slice(1), dropping the first row. The specification requires that rendering preserves every input row in order. This change causes the first row to be omitted.
findings.failure_scenario: When rendering a report with rows ['first', 'second'], the output will be ['second'] instead of ['first', 'second'], breaking the contract.
findings.title: Return all input rows to preserve order

findings.body: The code imports execSync and later uses it to run the report command. execSync invokes a shell, which violates the specification that report commands shall avoid shell interpretation. This can lead to shell injection vulnerabilities.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName containing shell metacharacters, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Use spawnSync instead of execSync to avoid shell interpretation

findings.body: Using execSync with a command string that includes untrusted userName allows shell injection. The command string is built with a template literal, so an attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands. Use spawnSync with an args array or sanitize the input.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker passes a userName containing shell metacharacters, execSync will execute them, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by avoiding shell interpolation

findings.body: The function returns rows.slice(1), dropping the first row, violating spec that rendering should preserve every input row.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows has more than one element, the first row is omitted from output, causing data loss.
findings.title: Return all rows, not drop first

findings.body: execSync spawns a shell and buffers output, which is slower than spawnSync. The original code used spawnSync.
findings.failure_scenario: When the command is run many times, execSync adds overhead.
findings.title: Use spawnSync instead of execSync for performance

findings.body: The code now invokes /bin/sh -c to run the report command, passing the user name via shell interpolation. The specification requires passing user names as process arguments without a shell, so this change introduces a shell dependency and potential injection risk.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker could supply a user name containing shell metacharacters, leading to command injection. The report command may be executed with unintended arguments, causing security breach.
findings.title: Use shell to execute report command; violates spec

findings.body: The method returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()), which removes the first element, violating the intent to preserve report rows. It also throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when rows is empty.
findings.failure_scenario: When render is called with a list of rows, the returned list will be missing the first row, causing incorrect report data. If rows is empty, the method will throw an exception.
findings.title: Do not drop the first row; preserve all rows

findings.body: The test only checks that the result is non‑null, not that it contains the expected rows. This removes coverage for the regression that drops the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: If the implementation changes to omit the first row, the test will still pass, allowing the bug to go unnoticed.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies returned rows

findings.body: The call to ioutil.ReadFile ignores the returned error, which can hide file read failures. Ignoring errors can lead to silent failures and hard-to-diagnose bugs.
findings.failure_scenario: ReadFile fails (e.g., defaults.json missing), error is ignored, function returns User and timeout regardless, leading to silent failure and potential downstream errors.
findings.suggestion: if _, err := ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json"); err != nil { /* handle error */ }
findings.title: Handle error from ioutil.ReadFile

findings.anchor: // FetchUser returns one user while preserving the stable User contract.
findings.body: The comment that documented FetchUser was removed, leaving the function undocumented. This can confuse users and violates documentation consistency.
findings.suggestion: // FetchUser returns a User and the timeout value used.
findings.title: Add missing docstring for FetchUser

findings.body: The function uses time.Duration but the time package is not imported, causing a compile error.
findings.failure_scenario: Compiling the package will fail with undefined type 'time.Duration'.
findings.title: Missing import for time package

findings.anchor: func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration) {
findings.body: The function signature changed from accepting a *time.Duration and returning a User to accepting a time.Duration and returning (User, time.Duration). This breaking change removes backward compatibility and requires callers to update their code. No tests cover the new return value, increasing risk of regressions.
findings.failure_scenario: Caller passes nil *time.Duration, causing compile error; function now returns two values, breaking code that expects a single User return.
findings.title: Add wrapper to preserve old FetchUser signature

findings.body: The function returns the timeout value that is identical to the input, which is redundant and may confuse callers.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers may misinterpret the second return value as a modified timeout.
findings.title: Return timeout value is redundant
